The winds were cold, leaves were falling fast, and three large boats left Lake-town, laden with rowers, Dwarves, a Hobbit, and hope.
Before the spider knew what was happening, it felt Bilbo's sting and rolled off the branch, dead.
Clever and cruel, Goblins were particularly good at making instruments of torture and destruction.
Not even the ravens knew of their coming until they arrived in the broken lands which divided the Lonely Mountain from the hills behind.

It was deep, deep dark, such as only Goblins that have taken to living in the heart of the mountain can see through.

"Alas! Bolg of the North is coming!"
—Gandalf
The rage of the wolves was terrible to see, and the commotion they made filled all the forest.
He rowed about quietly on the lake. Never a ripple did he make, not he.
"Where iss it? Losst it is, my precious!"

"If one were to sting me, I should swell up as big again as I am!"
—Bilbo
The Wargs planned to come by night upon the villages nearest the mountains. If their plan had been carried out, there would have been none left there next day.
"Old fool!" Bilbo thought. "Why, there is a large patch in the hollow of his left breast as bare as a snail out of its shell!"
"What shall we do?" cried Bilbo. "Escaping Goblins to be caught by wolves!"
The Goblin army poured in, driving wildly between the arms of the Mountain, seeking for the foe.
Goblins and wolves returned to the assault and soon forced their foes into a great ring, hemmed on all sides.
The grey chief spoke in their dreadful language, and every now and then all the Wargs in the circle would answer together.
It took more than Bilbo showing up alive to convince some that he was not, in fact, "presumed dead."

"I will prepare something particularly uncomfortable for you, Thorin Oakenshield!"
—The Great Goblin
With the Goblins pinching and laughing at them unmercifully, Bilbo wished again and again for his nice bright Hobbit hole. Not for the last time.
The spiders laughed. "You were quite right," they said, "the meat's alive and kicking!"
Bombur was always trying to recapture the beautiful dreams he had in the forest.
The Goblins began to sing, or croak, keeping time with the flap of their flat feet on the stone.

Fight wild Were-worms in the Last Desert
—Expression meaning "an impossible task"
At the twanging of the bows and the shrilling of the trumpets, the Dragon's wrath blazed to its height, till he was blind and mad with it.
"I can't be always carrying burglars on my back, down tunnels and up trees! What do you think I am? A porter?"
There rose from across the valley a deep-throated roar. With cries of "Moria!" and "Dáin, Dáin!" the Dwarves of the Iron Hills plunged in.
Gandalf thought of most things; and though he could not do everything, he could do a great deal for friends in a tight corner.

"I do hope I put the lids on tight enough!"
—Bilbo
Goblins made no beautiful things, but they made many clever ones.
Goblins had a simple approach to ownership: whatever you could hold onto was yours.
Their fires caught the attention of huge bats flapping and whirring round their ears.

When the heart of a Dwarf is wakened by gold, he grows suddenly bold and fierce.
The pinecones burst on the ground in the middle of the circle of wolves and went off in colored sparks and smoke.
Spears served Goblins better than swords or bows—they were quick to make and quiet to use.

n: Smaug, the Great Calamity // Spew Flame

faces.f: "My armor is like tenfold shields, my teeth are swords, my wings a hurricane, and my breath death!"
"You think you will get a fair share? If you get off alive, you will be lucky."
The Dwarves had barely time to fly back to the tunnel when Smaug came hurtling from the north, licking the mountainsides with flame, beating his great wings with a noise like a roaring wind.
Goblins did not usually venture very far from their mountains except to go on raids or hunt for food.
The stone-giants were out and were hurling rocks at one another for a game.
"To me! O my kinsfolk!"
Soon there came the sound of "Lazy Lob" and "Attercop" from among the trees away on the right. That upset the spiders greatly.

The guards were decidedly less than pleased, upon waking, to find their prisoners escaped.

"There must have been a regular bears' meeting outside here last night."
—Gandalf

"Here's the old villain with his head on a jug! He's been having a little feast all to himself!"
—Elven guard
Wargs and Goblins had few predators in the foothills of the Misty Mountains, but they did have some.
The Wood-Elves were not wicked folk. If they had a fault, it was distrust of strangers. Though their magic was strong, even in those days they were wary.
Even the littlest bears joined in important bear meetings and moonlit dances.
In the wide world, the Wood-Elves lingered in the twilight of the sun and moon but loved best the stars. They wandered in the great forests that grew tall in lands that were now lost.
Beorn's fences kept out Goblins and unwanted intruders, not hungry rabbits.
Since Bilbo was presumed dead, his belongings were auctioned by three of the town's best lawyers: Messrs. Grubb, Grubb, and Burrowes.

"Old Tomnoddy can't spy me!"
—Bilbo

"I should say there were little bears, large bears, ordinary bears, and gigantic big bears, all dancing outside from dark to nearly dawn."
—Gandalf
The shoving and name-calling was all in good fun, and Bilbo began to finally view the Dwarves as companions instead of strangers.

"Perhaps you have heard of my good cousin Radagast who lives near the southern borders of Mirkwood?" Gandalf asked.
"Yes," said Beorn, "not a bad fellow as Wizards go, I believe."

"Well, here is Mirkwood—the greatest of the forests of the northern world. I hope you like the look of it."
—Gandalf
Suddenly they were fighting like dogs, and calling one another all sorts of perfectly true and applicable names in very loud voices.
From infancy, Warg pups were taught to hunt and harry and to fear and hate the presence of Humans.
Wargs had little trouble devouring and digesting the most putrid of carcasses.
After the coming of Humans, the Wood-Elves took ever more and more to the gloaming and the dusk. Still Elves they were and remained—that is, Good People.
No one had dared to face the Dragon for many an age; nor would they have dared now, if it hadn't been for the grim-voiced Bard urging them on.
Tidings they had gathered in secret ways; and in all the mountains there was a forging and an arming.
Even magic rings were not much use against wolves—especially against the evil packs that lived near Goblin-infested mountains.
Seldom did Wargs venture near the dwellings of Humans, preferring instead to hunt and den over the Edge of the Wild.
Packs of evil wolves lived under the shadow of the Goblin-infested mountains, over the Edge of the Wild on the borders of the unknown.
The Company had lost a great deal, but they had killed the Great Goblin and many others besides. All in all, they had the best of it.
"Don't pinch! You need not be frightened like a rabbit. What is finer than flying?"
Out jumped the Goblins: big Goblins, small Goblins, great ugly-looking Goblins, lots of Goblins!

"I followed these bear tracks as far as the Carrock. There they disappeared into the river, but the water was too deep and strong beyond the rock for me to cross."
—Gandalf

"Merry be the greenwood, while the world is yet young! And merry be all your folk!"
—Gandalf

"If more of us valued food and cheer and song above hoarded gold, it would be a merrier world."
—Thorin
Lake-town was much diminished from its old grandeur, but still the Long Lake provided for all their needs.
In a great hall with pillars hewn out of the living stone sat the Elvenking on a chair of carven wood.
They escaped at times to ride or run over open lands by moonlight or starlight.
Suddenly a sword flashed in its own light.

"I forgot to mention that with the map went a key, a small and curious key."
—Gandalf, to Thorin
"It won't see us, will it, my precious?"
"Stand by the grey stone when the thrush knocks," read Elrond, "and the setting sun with the last light of Durin's Day will shine upon the keyhole."
"Put on a few eggs, there's a good fellow!" -Gandalf, to Bilbo
Filled with the twinkling lights, laughter, and songs of the Elves.
Elf-guards sang as they marched along the twisting, crossing, and echoing paths.
The passages were crossed and tangled in all directions, and it was most horribly stuffy.
In a hole in the ground there lived a Hobbit . . .
The hills provided quality iron, allowing Dáin's folk to clad themselves in hauberks of steel mail and hoses of fine metal mesh.
The Elves spoke of a strange town built right on the surface of the Long Lake, under the shadow of the Dragon-mountain.

"Stick to the forest-track, keep your spirits up, and hope for the best."
—Gandalf

Roads go ever ever on
Under cloud and under star,
Yet feet that wandering have gone
Turn at last to home afar.

The streams shall run in gladness,
The lakes shall shine and burn,
And sorrow fail and sadness
At the Mountain-king's return!

The wind went on from west to east;
All movement in the forest ceased,
But shrill and harsh across the marsh
Its whistling voices were released.

Far over the misty mountains cold
To dungeons deep and caverns old
We must away, ere break of day,
To seek the pale enchanted gold.

Sigh no more Pine, till the wind of the morn!
Fall Moon! Dark be the land!
Hush! Hush! Oak, Ash, and Thorn!
Hushed be all water, till dawn is at hand!

"Slash them! Beat them! Bite them! Gnash them!"

Where is the helm and the hauberk,
and the bright hair flowing?"

and cold be sleep under stone:
never more to wake on stony bed,

—Gandalf
